2Ki 21:7.rationale: God's promise to establish his Name forever in the temple and Jerusalem, chosen out of all Israel's tribes.

Heb 1:2.rationale: Aiōnas here means 'the universe/worlds' made through the Son; nothing is called eternal.

Heb 1:8.rationale: Addressed explicitly to the Son: 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever.'

Heb 1:12.rationale: Psalm about the LORD applied to the Son: 'Your years will never end'; could be read under God, but the context addresses the Son.

2Ch 21:7.rationale: God promised to maintain a lamp for David and his descendants forever, grounded in the Davidic covenant; the lamp/house is the thing said to endure.

Eze 25:4.rationale: Qedem here means 'the East' as a direction (people of the East), not eternity.

Eze 25:10.rationale: Qedem is directional ('people of the East'); 'no longer be remembered' is not phrased as forever.

Eze 25:15.rationale: 'Olam' describes the Philistines' long-standing ('ancient', often 'perpetual') hostility, meaning mere antiquity of human enmity, not eternity. Otherwise it would fall under Men, human things.

Pr 12:19.rationale: Proverbial saying that truthful lips endure forever, contrasted with a lying tongue's moment; a human matter, though it could be read as a blessing of the righteous.

Mk 11:14.rationale: Greek eis ton aiōna: the fig tree is cursed never to bear fruit again, a lasting judgment enacted on a symbol of fruitless Israel; alternatively merely an idiom 'ever again'.

Rev 4:9.rationale: The One seated on the throne is described as he 'who lives forever and ever', God's own eternal life.

Rev 4:10.rationale: The elders worship 'Him who lives forever and ever', ascribing eternal life to God himself.

Mt 13:22.rationale: αἰών here means 'this life/age' (worries of this age), not eternity.

Mt 13:39.rationale: 'End of the age' marks the close of the present age, not anything called eternal.

Mt 13:40.rationale: 'End of the age' refers to the harvest time; burning is not described as eternal here.

Mt 13:49.rationale: 'End of the age' denotes the final judgment's timing, not eternity.

Ro 6:22.rationale: The outcome of being slaves to God is 'eternal life', life God gives to believers.

Ro 6:23.rationale: 'The gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus', eternal life given to believers, contrasted with death as sin's wages.

Heb 11:3.rationale: Aiōnas here means 'the universe/worlds' (ages as created realms), not a statement that anything is eternal or everlasting.

Eze 38:8.rationale: תָּמִיד here describes the mountains of Israel as having been 'long/continually' desolate, a past duration, not anything declared eternal or everlasting.

Ezr 4:15.rationale: Aramaic 'alam here means 'from ancient times', describing Jerusalem's past rebellion; mere antiquity, not eternity.

Ezr 4:19.rationale: 'From ancient times' refers to the city's historical revolts, expressing antiquity only, not anything lasting forever.

Ps 83:17.rationale: Imprecation that Israel's enemies be ashamed and terrified 'forever' (la'ad-ad); lasting shame on the wicked, though v16 hopes they seek God's name, softening permanence.

Isa 19:11.rationale: קֶדֶם here means 'eastern' or 'ancient' kings, mere antiquity or direction, not eternity.

Ge 8:22.rationale: God promises the natural cycles of seasons and day and night 'shall never cease' while earth endures—a lasting decree for the created order, though bounded by 'as long as the earth endures'.

Ps 85:5.rationale: The psalmist asks whether God will be angry forever and draw out his anger to all generations, a rhetorical question expecting restoration.

Ro 12:2.rationale: Aiōn here means 'this age/world', the present order believers must not conform to; nothing is called eternal or lasting forever.

Eze 16:55.rationale: "Former state" (qadmah) denotes mere prior condition, not eternity.

Eze 16:60.rationale: God promises to establish an everlasting covenant with Jerusalem, remembering the covenant of her youth.

Ge 3:22.rationale: The tree of life would let the man 'live forever'; it is a hypothetical, withheld eternal life, closest to life God gives, though not promised to believers here.

Ge 3:24.rationale: Qedem here means 'east', a direction, not eternity.

Ps 131:3.rationale: "Forevermore" marks the duration of Israel's exhortation to hope in the LORD, not a claim that any person or thing is eternal; at most an adverbial idiom.

Ex 38:13.rationale: Qedem here means the east side of the courtyard, a mere direction, not eternity.

Ne 2:3.rationale: Nehemiah uses the court formula "May the king live forever" to Artaxerxes, a loose human use of 'forever'.

Da 9:24.rationale: The seventy weeks culminate in God bringing in "everlasting righteousness" alongside atonement for iniquity, a saving righteousness he provides that is called everlasting.

1Ti 6:12.rationale: Timothy is urged to take hold of the eternal life to which he was called.

Ps 12:7.rationale: The LORD will forever guard his people from this generation: lasting security promised to the godly. Could alternatively be read as God's faithfulness.

Mt 25:46.rationale: The verse makes two separate statements: the wicked go into eternal punishment, and the righteous go into eternal life.

Dt 31:13.rationale: "As long as you live in the land" (all the days) is a temporal limit on Israel's residence, not a claim that anything is eternal.

Ps 109:15.rationale: Tamid here means 'always/continually' before the LORD, an imprecation of ongoing remembrance rather than a statement of eternity.

Ps 109:19.rationale: BSB renders tamid 'forever': the curse is to cling permanently to the wicked accuser; the Hebrew tamid may mean only 'continually', so relevance is doubtful.

Lev 7:36.rationale: The priestly portion is called a permanent statute/portion for the generations to come.

Jer 3:5.rationale: The people ask whether God will be angry forever or indignant to the end, the exact question this heading covers.

Jer 3:12.rationale: God declares, "I will not be angry forever," denying that his anger lasts forever, on the ground of his mercy.

Isa 26:4.rationale: The LORD is called "the Rock eternal" (tsur olamim), describing God himself as everlasting; "trust forever" is the believers' response, not a separate heading.

Job 7:16.rationale: Job says he would not live forever; this is a negated wish in his lament, and nothing is actually called eternal. It could arguably go under 'Men, human things?'.

1Co 9:25.rationale: The believer's crown is called imperishable (aphthartos), contrasted with a perishable wreath: a lasting reward promised to God's people; inclusion depends on counting 'imperishable' as never ending.

Ps 139:5.rationale: Qedem here means 'before/in front' (hem me in behind and before), a direction, not eternity.

Ps 73:12.rationale: 'Always carefree' (olam) describes the wicked's ongoing ease, not something eternal; mere duration idiom.

Ps 73:23.rationale: Tamid 'always/continually' describes habitual presence, not eternity.

Ps 73:26.rationale: God is the psalmist's portion forever, a lasting blessing to the believer; could alternatively be read as God's eternal faithfulness.

Jer 52:34.rationale: A daily allowance 'until the day of his death' is bounded by a lifetime; the word denotes regularity, not anything lasting forever.

Ps 93:5.rationale: Holiness adorns God's house "for length of days" (forevermore), a lasting holiness of the temple; the testimonies clause is not itself said to be forever.

Ps 61:4.rationale: The psalmist asks to dwell in God's tent forever, a lasting blessing of dwelling with God.

Ps 61:6.rationale: Prayer that the king's years span many generations ('generation and generation'); could be royal court hyperbole (Men, human things) or messianic hope.

Ps 61:7.rationale: The Davidic king is to sit enthroned before God forever; some read it messianically (Jesus, the Son) or as court formula.
